questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x^3\,dy+(xy-1)\,dx=0$, $x>0$, $y\left(\frac12\right)=3-e$. Then $y(1)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Divide by $x^3\,dx$ to get a linear equation; the integral of $e^{-1/x}/x^3$ falls to the substitution $t=-1/x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Change the variable to $u=1/x$: the equation becomes constant-coefficient, solved by a particular solution plus the complementary solution.
solution: Try the particular solution $y=au+b$: $a-(au+b)=-u$ gives $a=1,\ b=1$, so $y_p=u+1$.
The complementary solution of $\frac{dy}{du}-y=0$ is $Ce^{u}$, so $y=u+1+Ce^{u}=\frac1x+1+Ce^{1/x}$.

useful_results: For $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$ with $P=\frac1{x^2}$: $\int P\,dx=-\frac1x$, so the integrating factor is $e^{-1/x}$ and the complementary solution is $Ce^{1/x}$.
Substituting $u=\frac1x$ turns $y'+\frac{y}{x^2}=\frac1{x^3}$ into the constant-coefficient equation $y_u-y=-u$; look for a polynomial particular solution of the same degree as the right side.
$\int t\,e^{t}dt=(t-1)e^{t}+C$ is the integral that appears whenever the right side is a power times an exponential.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(x^2-3y^2)\,dx+3xy\,dy=0$, $y(1)=1$. Then $6y^2(e)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The equation has only $y^2$ and $x$: put $t=y^2$ to get a linear equation in $t$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The equation is homogeneous, so put $y=vx$; the variables separate immediately.

useful_results: If $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ is homogeneous, $y=vx$ always separates: $\frac{dx}{x}=-\frac{N\,dv}{M+vN}$ (after cancelling $x^{n}$).
If $y$ occurs only as $y^2$ (and $y\,dy$), try $t=y^2$: $y\,dy=\frac12dt$ gives a linear equation in $t$.
Instance here: $(x^2-3y^2)dx+3xy\,dy=0$ gives $\frac{y^2}{x^2}=1-\frac23\ln x$ with $y(1)=1$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac yx\left(1+xy^2(1+\log_ex)\right)$, $x>0$, $y(1)=3$. Then $\frac{y^2(x)}{9}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Dividing by $y^3$ and putting $t=\frac1{y^2}$ turns the Bernoulli equation into a linear one.
solution: Let $\frac1{y^2}=t$, so $-\frac2{y^3}\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dt}{dx}$. Then $-\frac12\frac{dt}{dx}-\frac tx=1+\ln x$, i.e. $\frac{dt}{dx}+\frac{2t}{x}=-2(1+\ln x)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The combination $z=\frac{x^2}{y^2}$ makes the equation separable at once - no integrating factor.
solution: So $z'=-2x^2(1+\ln x)$: the right side has no $y$.

useful_results: Bernoulli equation $y'+Py=Qy^n$ ($n\ne1$): put $t=y^{1-n}$, which gives the linear equation $t'+(1-n)Pt=(1-n)Q$. Here $n=3$, $t=y^{-2}$.

If $y'=\frac yx+(\text{function of }x)\,y^3$, the combination $\frac{x^2}{y^2}$ (i.e. $(y/x)^{-2}$) is the natural variable: $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^2}{y^2}\right)=-2x^2\,g(x)$ for $y'=\frac yx+g(x)\,y^3$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(t)$ be a solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dt}+\alpha y=\gamma e^{-\beta t}$, where $\alpha>0,\beta>0$ and $\gamma>0$. Then $\lim_{t\to\infty}y(t)$
questions.key_idea: Solve the linear equation; every term of $y(t)$ contains a decaying exponential.
solution: $y\,e^{\alpha t}=\int e^{\alpha t}\cdot\gamma e^{-\beta t}dt+c=\gamma\int e^{(\alpha-\beta)t}dt+c$.
If $\alpha=\beta$: $y\,e^{\alpha t}=\gamma t+c$, so $y=(\gamma t+c)e^{-\alpha t}\to0$ as well. Hence the limit is $0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF divides by (alpha - beta), so it silently assumes alpha != beta. Working and answer are right for alpha != beta; the case alpha = beta (where the integral gives gamma*t) was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: No formula needed: squeeze the solution between $0$ and a number as small as we like, using only that the forcing term tends to $0$.
solution: Since $\gamma e^{-\beta t}>0$, $y'+\alpha y>0$, i.e. $(ye^{\alpha t})'>0$, so $y(t)e^{\alpha t}\ge y(0)$ for $t\ge0$ and hence $y(t)\ge y(0)e^{-\alpha t}\to0$. So $\liminf y\ge0$.
Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $T$ with $\gamma e^{-\beta t}<\varepsilon$ for $t>T$. Then $y'+\alpha y<\varepsilon$ for $t>T$.

Multiply by $e^{\alpha t}$: $\left(ye^{\alpha t}\right)'<\varepsilon e^{\alpha t}$; integrating from $T$ to $t$: $y(t)<\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}+\left(y(T)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\right)e^{-\alpha(t-T)}$.
Hence $\limsup y\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so $\limsup y\le0$.

useful_results: For $y'+\alpha y=g(t)$ with $\alpha>0$ and $g(t)\to0$, every solution tends to $0$ (stable linear system: transients $e^{-\alpha t}$ die out and follow the forcing).
If $g\to L$ instead, $y\to L/\alpha$; e.g. $y'+\alpha y=\gamma$ has $y\to\gamma/\alpha$.
$\int e^{kt}dt=\frac{e^{kt}}{k}$ for $k\ne0$ but $=t$ for $k=0$ - always check the resonant case $\alpha=\beta$.

questions.question: Let $y=f(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $y(x+1)\,dx-x^2dy=0$, $y(1)=e$. Then $\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Separate: $\frac{dy}{y}=\left(\frac1x+\frac1{x^2}\right)dx$; then the $-\frac1x$ in the exponent sends $y\to0$ as $x\to0^+$.
solution: $\ln x-\frac1x=\ln y-2$, so $\ln y=\ln x-\frac1x+2$, i.e. $y=e^{\ln x-\frac1x+2}=x\,e^{2-\frac1x}$.
As $x\to0^+$: $\ln x\to-\infty$ and $-\frac1x\to-\infty$, so the exponent $\to-\infty$ and $e^{-\infty}=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the definite integral from the initial point: $\ln y$ is a divergent integral of a positive function, so no closed form is needed.
solution: The integrand is positive on $(0,1]$ and $\int_x^1\frac{dt}{t^2}=\frac1x-1\to\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ (also $\int_x^1\frac{dt}{t}=-\ln x\to\infty$).

useful_results: For $\frac{dy}{y}=g(x)\,dx$, $y(x)=y(x_0)\exp\left(\int_{x_0}^xg\right)$; the limit at an endpoint is decided by whether $\int g$ diverges to $\pm\infty$.
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+1}{x^2}y$ always has solution $y=Cx\,e^{-1/x}$ ($x>0$), which $\to0$ as $x\to0^+$ because $e^{-1/x}$ beats any power of $x$.
Check the answer: $y(1)=C\cdot1\cdot e^{-1}=e$ gives $C=e^2$, so $f(x)=e^{2}x\,e^{-1/x}$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x\log_ex\frac{dy}{dx}+y=x^2\log_ex$, $(x>1)$. If $y(2)=2$, then $y(e)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: After dividing by $x\ln x$ the integrating factor is $\ln x$, and $\int x\ln x\,dx$ is by parts.
solution: Divide by $x\ln x$: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x\ln x}=x$, a linear equation.
Integrating factor: $e^{\int\frac{dx}{x\ln x}}=e^{\ln(\ln x)}=\ln x$ (as $x>1$, $\ln x>0$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot that the left side is exact, $\frac{d}{dx}(y\ln x)=\ln x\,y'+\frac yx$, and integrate between the two given points - no constant to find.
solution: Divide the equation by $x$: $\ln x\,\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x\ln x$. The left side is $\frac{d}{dx}(y\ln x)$ (product rule).

useful_results: For $y'+Py=Q$ with $P=\frac{f'}{f}$ the integrating factor is simply $f$, because $f\,y'+f'y=(fy)'$. Here $f=\ln x$ and $P=\frac1{x\ln x}$.
Using $\int_{x_0}^{x}$ with the given point removes the constant of integration entirely.

questions.question: Let the solution curve $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{3x^5\tan^{-1}(x^3)}{(1+x^6)^{3/2}}y=2x\exp\left\{\frac{x^3-\tan^{-1}x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^6}}\right\}$ pass through the origin. Then $y(1)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: With $t=\tan^{-1}x^3$ the integrating factor becomes $e^{t\cos t-\sin t}$, which cancels the exponential on the right.
solution: Let $\tan^{-1}x^3=t$, so $x^3=\tan t$, $\frac{3x^2}{1+x^6}dx=dt$ and $\sqrt{1+x^6}=\sec t$. The integral becomes $\int\frac{\tan t}{\sec t}\,t\,dt=\int t\sin t\,dt$.
So $\text{I.F.}=e^{-\int t\sin t\,dt}=e^{t\cos t-\sin t}$ (since $\int t\sin t\,dt=-t\cos t+\sin t$).
useful_results: For $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$, if $Q(x)=g(x)\,e^{\int P}$-type exponentials appear, the integrating factor $e^{\int P}$ often cancels them exactly; check this before integrating.
With $t=\tan^{-1}x^3$ (i.e. $x^3=\tan t$): $\sin t=\frac{x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^6}}$, $\cos t=\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^6}}$, $dt=\frac{3x^2dx}{1+x^6}$.
$\int t\sin t\,dt=\sin t-t\cos t+C$.
Check: $g(x)=\frac{x^3-\tan^{-1}x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^6}}=\sin t-t\cos t$ has $g'(x)=P(x)$, so $y=x^2e^{g}$ solves the equation.

questions.question: The solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\left(\frac{x^2+3y^2}{3x^2+y^2}\right)$, $y(1)=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: Homogeneous equation: $y=vx$ gives $\frac{v^2+3}{(v+1)^3}$, which splits into three simple fractions in $v+1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For a homogeneous $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$, $\frac1{xM+yN}$ is an integrating factor; here it is $\frac1{(x+y)^3}$, and the exact equation is integrated by inspection.
solution: Write $(x^2+3y^2)dx+(3x^2+y^2)dy=0$; $M=x^2+3y^2$, $N=3x^2+y^2$ are homogeneous of degree 2 and $M_y=6y\ne N_x=6x$.
$xM+yN=x^3+3xy^2+3x^2y+y^3=(x+y)^3$, so multiply by $\frac1{(x+y)^3}$ to make the equation exact.
Check that $\varphi=\ln|x+y|+\frac{2xy}{(x+y)^2}$ has $\varphi_x=\frac1{x+y}+\frac{2y(x+y)-4xy}{(x+y)^3}=\frac{x^2+3y^2}{(x+y)^3}$, and by symmetry $\varphi_y=\frac{3x^2+y^2}{(x+y)^3}$.
So the general solution is $\ln|x+y|+\frac{2xy}{(x+y)^2}=c$; $y(1)=0$ gives $c=0$, option (C).

useful_results: For a homogeneous equation $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ with $xM+yN\neq0$, $\frac{1}{xM+yN}$ is an integrating factor (Euler).
Recognise $x^3+3x^2y+3xy^2+y^3=(x+y)^3$: the denominator after $y=vx$ is $(v+1)^3$, signalling partial fractions in $v+1$.
Partial fractions shortcut: expand the numerator in powers of the repeated factor, $v^2+3=(v+1)^2-2(v+1)+4$.

questions.question: Let a differentiable function $f$ satisfy $f(x)+\int_3^x\frac{f(t)}{t}dt=\sqrt{x+1}$, $x\ge3$. Then $12f(8)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $x=3$ to get $f(3)=2$, differentiate to get a linear equation with integrating factor $x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Work with $F(x)=\int_3^x\frac{f(t)}{t}dt$: since $f=xF'$, the equation becomes $(xF)'=\sqrt{x+1}$, which integrates directly.

useful_results: For $f(x)+\int_a^xg\,f=h(x)$ type equations: put $x=a$ to get the initial value, differentiate to get a first-order linear DE.
If $f=xF'$ and the equation reads $xF'+F$, the left side is $(xF)'$ - the integrating factor $x$ is built in.
Check: $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}\left(\frac{(x+1)^{3/2}}{3}-\sqrt{x+1}+\frac{16}{3}\right)$ gives $f(3)=2$ and $f(8)=\frac{17}{12}$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(3y^2-5x^2)y\,dx+2x(x^2-y^2)\,dy=0$ such that $y(1)=1$. Then $|(y(2))^3-12y(2)|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: With $y=tx$ the numerator becomes $3t-t^3$, whose derivative is $3(1-t^2)$: the integral is a logarithm.
solution: Let $3t-t^3=z$, so $dz=3(1-t^2)dt$. Then $\frac23\int\frac{dz}{z}=\ln x+c$, i.e. $\frac23\ln|3t-t^3|=\ln x+c$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working stops after the substitution 3t - t^3 = z (the page ends there); the remaining steps (integration, constant, back-substitution, evaluation at x = 2) were completed. The answer A is correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot the combination $u=3x^2y-y^3$: $du=6xy\,dx+3(x^2-y^2)dy$ is half of the equation's second term, so the equation becomes $\frac{du}{u}=\frac{9}{2x}dx$.
solution: At $x=2$: $|y^3-12y|=2\cdot2^{9/2}=32\sqrt2$ - the quantity asked is exactly $|u|$ at $x=2$.

useful_results: For a homogeneous equation $y=tx$ gives $x\frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{N(t)}{D(t)}$; when $D'(t)$ is a multiple of $N$'s factor (here $\frac{d}{dt}(3t-t^3)=3(1-t^2)$) the integral is a pure logarithm.
Even when the solution is implicit, a question may ask only for a combination of it (here $y^3-12y$ at $x=2$): evaluate the first integral directly, do not solve for $y$.
The first integral here is $3x^2y-y^3=Cx^{9/2}$ (homogeneous of degree 3 in $x,y$ against $x^{9/2}$).

questions.question: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+y\tan x=x\sec x$, $0\le x\le\frac\pi3$, $y(0)=1$, then $y\left(\frac\pi6\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Integrating factor $\sec x$; then $\int x\sec^2x\,dx$ by parts.
solution: Solution: $y\sec x=\int x\sec x\cdot\sec x\,dx=\int x\sec^2x\,dx=x\tan x-\int\tan x\,dx$.
useful_results: If $P(x)=\tan x$ the integrating factor is $\sec x$; equivalently put $y=u\cos x$, which gives $u'\cos x=Q$.
$\int x\sec^2x\,dx=x\tan x+\ln|\cos x|+C$.
Sign-flip identity for the options: $a\ln b=-a\ln\frac1b$; match the form by writing the constant as $\ln e$.

questions.question: Let $\alpha x=\exp\left(x^\beta y^\gamma\right)$ be the solution of the differential equation $2x^2y\,dy-(1-xy^2)\,dx=0$, $x>0$, $y(2)=\sqrt{\log_e2}$. Then $\alpha+\beta-\gamma$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Put $y^2=t$: the equation becomes linear with integrating factor $x$, and $xy^2=\ln(2x)$ follows.
solution: Integrating factor: $e^{\ln x}=x$, so $xt=\int\frac1{x^2}\cdot x\,dx=\ln x+C$, i.e. $xy^2=\ln x+C$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The substitution $s=xy^2$ turns the equation into $x\,ds=dx$: $d(xy^2)=y^2dx+2xy\,dy$ appears inside it.

useful_results: Spot exact differentials: $y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy)$, $x\,dy-y\,dx=x^2d(y/x)$, $2xy\,dy+y^2dx=d(xy^2)$ (here $2xy\,dy=d(xy^2)-y^2dx$).
If an equation has $y$ only through $y^2$ and $y\,dy$, the substitution $y^2=t$ makes it linear (when the original is linear in $y^2$).
Check: $xy^2=\ln(2x)$ at $x=2$ gives $y^2=\frac{\ln4}{2}=\ln2$.

questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a differentiable function such that $f'(x)+f(x)=\int_0^2f(t)\,dt$. If $f(0)=e^{-2}$, then $2f(0)-f(2)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $\int_0^2f$ is a constant $k$; solve the linear equation in terms of $k$, then use the self-consistency $k=\int_0^2f$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Never find $f$: integrate the equation over $[0,2]$ and use that $f-k$ decays like $e^{-x}$; the required quantity is $f(0)-k$.
solution: But $f(2)-k=f(0)$ (from the first step), so $f(0)=(f(0)-k)e^{-2}$, i.e. $f(0)-k=e^{2}f(0)$.

useful_results: In $f'+f=\int_a^bf$ the integral is a constant $k$; $f-k=(f(a)-k)e^{-(x-a)}$ always.
Integrating $f'(x)=h(x)$ over $[a,b]$ gives $f(b)-f(a)$: this gives relations between endpoint values without solving.

concepts: Linear differential equations (with $x$ as dependent variable)
questions.question: If the solution curve $f(x,y)=0$ of the differential equation $(1+\log_ex)\frac{dx}{dy}-x\log_ex=e^y$, $x>0$, passes through the points $(1,0)$ and $(\alpha,2)$, then $\alpha^\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $(1+\ln x)\,dx=d(x\ln x)$, so $t=x\ln x$ gives a linear equation in $y$.
solution: The point $(1,0)$ gives $0=0+c$, so $c=0$ and $x\ln x=ye^y$.

alternate_solutions.idea: After $t=x\ln x$ the equation is $t'-t=e^y$, the resonant case: undetermined coefficients with $y\,e^y$ (no integrating factor).
solution: With $t=x\ln x$: $\frac{dt}{dy}-t=e^y$. The complementary solution of $t'-t=0$ is $Ce^y$.
Since $e^y$ already solves the homogeneous equation, try $t_p=ky\,e^y$: $t_p'-t_p=ke^y=e^y$, so $k=1$ and $t_p=ye^y$.

useful_results: $\frac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=1+\ln x$: a factor $(1+\ln x)$ multiplying $\frac{dx}{dy}$ signals $t=x\ln x$.
$\frac{dt}{dy}-t=e^y$ is the resonant case: the particular solution is $y\,e^y$, not $e^y$.
$\alpha^\alpha=e^{\alpha\ln\alpha}$: the answer needs only $\alpha\ln\alpha$, never $\alpha$ itself (it is $e^2$ here).

questions.question: The slope of tangent at any point $(x,y)$ on a curve $y=y(x)$ is $\frac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}$, $x>0$. If $y(2)=0$, then a value of $y(8)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Homogeneous equation: $y=vx$ separates as $\frac{2v\,dv}{1-v^2}=\frac{dx}{x}$.
solution: At $x=8$: $y^2-64=-16$, so $y^2=48$ and $y=4\sqrt3$ (the positive root is the listed option).

alternate_solutions.idea: The right side is $\frac x{2y}+\frac y{2x}$: with $t=y^2$ the equation is linear, $\left(\frac tx\right)'=1$.
solution: So $\frac{dt}{dx}-\frac tx=x$; the integrating factor is $\frac1x$, giving $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac tx\right)=1$.

useful_results: For $y'=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2xy}$ (an even function of $y$ in the numerator, $y$ in the denominator) the substitution $t=y^2$ gives the linear equation $t'=x+\frac tx$.
The general solution $y^2=x^2+Cx$, i.e. $\left(x+\frac C2\right)^2-y^2=\frac{C^2}{4}$, is a family of rectangular hyperbolas through the origin with centre on the $x$-axis.
The solution is unique only for $x$ away from $y=0$; the sign of $y$ is a branch choice, which is why the question asks for 'a value'.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be a solution curve of the differential equation $(1-x^2y^2)\,dx=y\,dx+x\,dy$. If the line $x=1$ intersects the curve $y=y(x)$ at $y=2$ and the line $x=2$ intersects the curve $y=y(x)$ at $y=\alpha$, then a value of $\alpha$ is:
questions.key_idea: $y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy)$, so $u=xy$ gives $\frac{du}{1-u^2}=dx$; partial fractions give a logarithm.
solution: Take the positive sign: $\frac{2\alpha+1}{2\alpha-1}=3e^2$, so $2\alpha+1=6e^2\alpha-3e^2$, i.e. $2\alpha(3e^2-1)=3e^2+1$.
The negative sign would need $xy<1$, i.e. $2\alpha<1$; but $u=xy$ starts at $2>1$ and cannot cross the constant solution $u=1$, so $u>1$ throughout and the positive sign is the correct one.

alternate_solutions.idea: The substitution $w=\frac{u+1}{u-1}$ (with $u=xy$) turns the equation into $w'=2w$: no logarithms and no cases.
solution: $u=xy$ satisfies $u'=1-u^2$. $u=1$ is a constant solution, so by uniqueness $u>1$ for all $x$ when $u(1)=2$.

useful_results: The combination $y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy)$: if the equation involves only $xy$ besides this, put $u=xy$.
$\frac{du}{1-u^2}=dx$ integrates to $\frac12\ln\left|\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right|=x+c$; the constant solutions $u=\pm1$ divide the plane into regions and a solution cannot leave its region.
The Möbius variable $w=\frac{u+1}{u-1}$ linearises $u'=1-u^2$ to $w'=2w$ (more generally $u'=a(u-p)(u-q)$ becomes $w'=a(p-q)w$ for $w=\frac{u-p}{u-q}$ up to sign).

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{5}{x(x^5+1)}y=\frac{(x^5+1)^2}{x^7}$, $x>0$. If $y(1)=2$, then $y(2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\frac{5}{x(x^5+1)}=\frac5x-\frac{5x^4}{x^5+1}$, so the integrating factor is $\frac{x^5}{1+x^5}$.
useful_results: In general $\int\frac{n\,dx}{x(x^n+1)}=\ln\frac{x^n}{1+x^n}+C$, from the partial fractions $\frac{n}{x(x^n+1)}=\frac nx-\frac{nx^{n-1}}{x^n+1}$ (here $n=5$).
If the right side is a perfect square over a power of $x$, multiply by the integrating factor first - the product often collapses to $x^a+x^b$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$, $y>0$, be a solution curve of the differential equation $(1+x^2)\,dy=y(x-y)\,dx$. If $y(0)=1$ and $y(2\sqrt2)=\beta$, then:
questions.key_idea: Divide by $y^2$ and put $t=\frac1y$ to get a linear equation with integrating factor $\sqrt{1+x^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The combination $s=\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{y}$ has the derivative $\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ - the equation is a ready-made exact derivative.

useful_results: Bernoulli $y'+Py=Qy^n$: $t=y^{1-n}$ gives the linear equation $t'+(1-n)Pt=(1-n)Q$. Here $n=2$: $t=\frac1y$.
$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)+C=\sinh^{-1}x+C$.

questions.question: Let $y=y_1(x)$ and $y=y_2(x)$ be the solution curves of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=y+7$ with initial conditions $y_1(0)=0$ and $y_2(0)=1$ respectively. Then the curves $y=y_1(x)$ and $y=y_2(x)$ intersect at:
questions.key_idea: Both solutions are $-7+ce^x$ with different $c$; equal values force $e^x=0$.
solution: $e^x>0$ for all real $x$, so there is no solution: the curves do not intersect.

alternate_solutions.idea: Subtract the two solutions: $z=y_2-y_1$ satisfies $z'=z$, $z(0)=1$, so it is never zero (no solving of the main equation needed).
solution: $e^x>0$ for all $x$, so $y_2(x)\ne y_1(x)$ everywhere: no intersection point.

useful_results: For $y'=f(y)$ solutions cannot cross (uniqueness of the IVP): two solution curves of the same equation either coincide or never meet where the equation is regular.
The difference of two solutions of $y'+Py=Q$ solves the homogeneous equation $z'+Pz=0$, so is $Ce^{-\int P}$, which never vanishes unless $C=0$.
$y'=y+7$ has equilibrium $y=-7$; all other solutions move away: $y=-7+ce^x$.

concepts: Linear differential equations (with $x$ as dependent variable)
questions.question: Let $x=x(y)$ be the solution of the differential equation $2(y+2)\log_e(y+2)\,dx+\left(x+4-2\log_e(y+2)\right)dy=0$, $y>-1$ with $x\left(e^4-2\right)=1$. Then $x\left(e^9-2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $t=\ln(y+2)$, so $dy=(y+2)\,dt$; the equation is linear in $x$ with integrating factor $\sqrt t$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $t=s^2$: then $2t\frac{dx}{dt}+x$ becomes $s\frac{dx}{ds}+x=\frac{d}{ds}(sx)$, an exact derivative - no integrating factor.
solution: With $t=\ln(y+2)$ the equation is $2t\,x_t+x=2t-4$. Let $t=s^2$, so $x_t=\frac{x_s}{2s}$.

useful_results: If the equation is awkward in $y$ (dependent) but linear in $x$, treat $x$ as dependent: $\frac{dx}{dy}+P(y)x=Q(y)$.
The substitution $\sqrt t=s$ turns $2t\,x'+x$ into $\frac{d}{ds}(sx)$ (since $2t\frac{d}{dt}=s\frac{d}{ds}$).
Check: $x(t)=\frac23t-4+\frac{14}{3\sqrt t}$ gives $x(4)=1$ and $x(9)=\frac{32}{9}$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be a solution of the differential equation $(x\cos x)\,dy+(xy\sin x+y\cos x-1)\,dx=0$, $0<x<\frac\pi2$. If $\frac\pi3y\left(\frac\pi3\right)=\sqrt3$, then $\left|\frac\pi6y''\left(\frac\pi6\right)+2y'\left(\frac\pi6\right)\right|$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $xy''+2y'=(xy)''$; the closed form of $xy$ is $\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x$, so the quantity is $|{-}xy|$ at $\frac\pi6$.
solution: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{x\sin x+\cos x}{x\cos x}\right)y=\frac1{x\cos x}$, i.e. $\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\tan x+\frac1x\right)y=\frac1{x\cos x}$.
Hence $xy\sec x=\tan x+\sqrt3$, i.e. $xy=\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x$.
questions.correction_note: PDF answer key says 'B' for this numerical question (no options); the working gives 2. The PDF working also jumps from c = sqrt3 straight to 'Hence |...| = |-2| = 2'; the intermediate steps (closed form of xy, (xy)'' = -xy, value at pi/6) were added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $u=xy$ in the equation: it becomes $u'\cos x+u\sin x=1$, i.e. $(u\sec x)'=\sec^2x$ - the integrating factor is just $\sec x$.
solution: Write the equation as $\cos x\,(xy'+y)+x\sin x\cdot y=1$. With $u=xy$: $u'=xy'+y$ and $x\sin x\,y=u\sin x$.
So $u'\cos x+u\sin x=1$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dx}(u\sec x)=\sec^2x$ and $u\sec x=\tan x+c$, i.e. $u=\sin x+c\cos x$.
At $\frac\pi3$: $u=\frac\pi3y=\sqrt3=\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac c2$, so $c=\sqrt3$ and $u=\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x$.
The required quantity is $xy''+2y'=u''=-u$, and at $x=\frac\pi6$: $u=\frac12+\frac32=2$.

useful_results: $(xy)''=xy''+2y'$ and $(xy)'=xy'+y$: expressions like $xy''+2y'$ or $xy'+y$ are derivatives of $u=xy$ - substitute $u=xy$.
$a\sin x+b\cos x$ satisfies $u''=-u$; so for $u=\sin x+\sqrt3\cos x=2\sin(x+\frac\pi3)$ the quantity is $-u$.
The equation $\cos x\,u'+\sin x\,u=1$ is $(u\sec x)'=\sec^2x$ - the general solution of $u'+u\tan x=\sec x$.

questions.question: Let a curve $y=f(x)$, $x\in(0,\infty)$ pass through the points $P\left(1,\frac32\right)$ and $Q\left(a,\frac12\right)$. If the tangent at any point $R(b,f(b))$ to the given curve cuts the $y$-axis at the point $S(0,c)$ such that $bc=3$, then $(PQ)^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The $y$-intercept of the tangent gives $xf'-f=-\frac3x$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac fx\right)=-\frac3{x^3}$.
solution: The tangent at $R(b,f(b))$ is $y-f(b)=f'(b)(x-b)$. It passes through $S(0,c)$: $c-f(b)=-b\,f'(b)$.
The curve passes through $\left(1,\frac32\right)$: $\frac32=\frac32+\lambda$, so $\lambda=0$ and $f(b)=\frac{3}{2b}$, i.e. $f(x)=\frac{3}{2x}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF solves 'f(a)=1/2 => 1/2 = 3/(2b) => b = 3' (variable mislabelled: it is a = 3, since the point is Q(a, 1/2)), then writes 'c = 1' which is not needed. Variable corrected to a; the rest is unchanged. Answer 5 is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometric viewpoint: the tangent's $y$-intercept is $f-xf'$; try $f=\frac kx$ as a particular solution, and note the homogeneous solutions are lines through the origin.
solution: The $y$-intercept of the tangent at $x$ is $f-xf'$, so the condition is $f-xf'=\frac3x$.
The homogeneous equation $f-xf'=0$ means the tangent passes through the origin at every point: $f=\lambda x$.
Particular solution: $f=\frac kx$ gives $f-xf'=\frac kx+\frac kx=\frac{2k}x=\frac3x$, so $k=\frac32$.

useful_results: The tangent at $(x_0,f(x_0))$ meets the $y$-axis at $f(x_0)-x_0f'(x_0)$ and the $x$-axis at $x_0-\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}$.
$xf'-f=x^2\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac fx\right)$ - the 'intercept' expression is a derivative of $\frac fx$.
For $y$-intercept $=\frac{k}{x}$-type conditions, hyperbolas $xy=\text{const}$ appear: $f=\frac{c}{x}$ has $y$-intercept $\frac{2c}{x}$.

questions.question: If the solution curve of the differential equation $(y-2\log_ex)\,dx+\left(x\log_ex^2\right)dy=0$, $x>1$ passes through the points $\left(e,\frac43\right)$ and $\left(e^4,\alpha\right)$, then $\alpha$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $x\log_ex^2=2x\ln x$, so the equation is linear with integrating factor $\sqrt{\ln x}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $t=\ln x$ and then $t=s^2$: the left side becomes the exact derivative $\frac{d}{ds}(sy)$.

useful_results: For $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{2x\ln x}=\frac1x$: with $t=\ln x$, $2t\,y_t+y=2t$; $s=\sqrt t$ gives $(sy)_s=2s^2$.
$\int\frac{(\ln x)^n}{x}dx=\frac{(\ln x)^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$ for any real $n\ne-1$.
Note $\log_ex^2=2\ln x$ (for $x>1$ no absolute value issues).

concepts: Linear differential equations (with $x$ as dependent variable)
questions.question: Let the solution curve $x=x(y)$, $0<y<\frac\pi2$, of the differential equation $\left(\log_e(\cos y)\right)^2\cos y\,dx-\left(1+3x\log_e(\cos y)\right)\sin y\,dy=0$ satisfy $x\left(\frac\pi3\right)=\frac1{2\log_e2}$. If $x\left(\frac\pi6\right)=\frac1{\log_em-\log_en}$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime, then $mn$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Put $L=\ln\cos y$ so $dL=-\tan y\,dy$: the integrating factor is $L^3$ and the right side integrates to $-\frac{L^2}2$.
solution: Let $L=\ln\cos y$. The equation gives $\frac{dx}{dy}=\tan y\left(\frac{3x}{L}+\frac1{L^2}\right)$, i.e. $\frac{dx}{dy}-\frac{3\tan y}{L}x=\frac{\tan y}{L^2}$.
$x\ln^3\cos y=\int\frac{\tan y}{L^2}\cdot L^3dy=\int\tan y\,\ln\cos y\,dy=-\int t\,dt=-\frac{\ln^2\cos y}{2}+C$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess the form $x=\frac aL$ with $L=\ln\cos y$: it satisfies the equation for $a=-\frac12$ and the given condition, so by uniqueness it is the solution.
solution: The equation requires $\frac{dx}{dy}=\tan y\left(\frac{3a}{L^2}+\frac1{L^2}\right)=\frac{(3a+1)\tan y}{L^2}$, so $a=3a+1$, i.e. $a=-\frac12$.
Check the condition: $x\left(\frac\pi3\right)=-\frac1{2(-\ln2)}=\frac1{2\ln2}$ ✓. By uniqueness of the initial-value problem this is the solution.

useful_results: When the independent variable is hidden inside a function, change variable first: $L=\ln\cos y$ has $dL=-\tan y\,dy$.
For $\frac{dx}{dL}+\frac{3x}{L}=-\frac1{L^2}$ the integrating factor is $L^3$ and $(L^3x)'=-L$: so $x=-\frac1{2L}+\frac{C}{L^3}$.
The homogeneous part $\frac C{L^3}$ is nonzero for $C\ne0$, so a particular solution that already meets the initial condition is the solution (uniqueness).

questions.question: Let the tangent at any point $P$ on a curve passing through the points $(1,1)$ and $\left(\frac1{10},100\right)$, intersect positive $x$-axis and $y$-axis at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. If $PA:PB=1:k$ and $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $e^{\frac{dy}{dx}}=kx+\frac k2$, $y(0)=k$, then $4y(1)-5\log_e3$ is equal to ________.
questions.answer: $4+\ln3$ (≈ 5.10, not an integer; the key says Bonus)
questions.key_idea: $PA:PB=1:k$ fixes the intercepts, giving $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{ky}{x}$, i.e. $yx^k=C$; the two points give $k=2$.
solution: $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $PA:PB=1:k$, so $P=\frac{k\cdot A+1\cdot B}{k+1}$ and the $x$-coordinate gives $x=\frac{k\alpha}{k+1}$, i.e. $\alpha=\frac{k+1}{k}x$.
Hence $x\frac{dy}{dx}+ky=0$, i.e. $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac kxy=0$, with integrating factor $x^k$: $yx^k=C$.
$4y(1)-5\ln3=4+\ln3\approx5.10$: not an integer, which is why the key lists the question as Bonus.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use intercept form: the slope of the tangent $AB$ is $-\frac\beta\alpha$ with $\beta=(k+1)y$, $\alpha=\frac{(k+1)x}{k}$ - the differential equation is read off directly; the integral is a definite integral from $x=0$.
solution: The tangent is line $AB$ with slope $-\frac\beta\alpha=-\frac{(k+1)y}{(k+1)x/k}=-\frac{ky}{x}$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{ky}{x}$ and $yx^k=C$.

useful_results: If $P$ divides the intercept segment $AB$ so that $PA:PB=1:k$, then $P=\left(\frac{k}{k+1}\alpha,\frac{1}{k+1}\beta\right)$; the tangent slope is $-\frac\beta\alpha=-k\frac yx$.
$\frac{dy}{dx}=-k\frac yx$ gives $yx^k=C$: for $k=1$ this is the hyperbola $xy=C$ (the tangent's point of contact is the midpoint of the intercepts).
$\int\ln(ax+b)\,dx=\frac{ax+b}{a}\left(\ln(ax+b)-1\right)+C$.

questions.question: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{4x}{x^2-1}y=\frac{x+2}{(x^2-1)^{5/2}}$, $x>1$ such that $y(2)=\frac29\log_e(2+\sqrt3)$ and $y(\sqrt2)=\alpha\log_e(\sqrt\alpha+\beta)+\beta-\sqrt\gamma$, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb N$, then $\alpha\beta\gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The integrating factor is $(x^2-1)^2$, which turns the right side into $\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}$.
solution: The equation is linear in $y$. Integrating factor: $e^{\int\frac{4x}{x^2-1}dx}=e^{2\ln(x^2-1)}=(x^2-1)^2$.
useful_results: $\frac{4x}{x^2-1}=2\cdot\frac{(x^2-1)'}{x^2-1}$, so the integrating factor is $(x^2-1)^2$; in general $\frac{k\,u'}{u}$ gives $u^k$.
$\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)+C$ and $\int\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}=\sqrt{x^2-1}+C$.
Matching forms: $2\ln(\sqrt2+1)=\alpha\ln(\sqrt\alpha+\beta)$ with $\alpha=2,\beta=1$ because $\sqrt2+1$ is the unique form $\sqrt\alpha+\beta$ with natural $\alpha,\beta$ giving this coefficient.

questions.question: Let $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t)$ be solutions of the differential equations $\frac{dx}{dt}+ax=0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt}+by=0$ respectively, $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Given that $x(0)=2$; $y(0)=1$ and $3y(1)=2x(1)$, the value of $t$, for which $x(t)=y(t)$, is:
questions.key_idea: Both are exponentials; the condition $3y(1)=2x(1)$ fixes $e^{a-b}=\frac43$, which is all that is needed.
solution: $\frac{dx}{dt}=-ax$ gives $\int\frac{dx}x=-\int a\,dt$, so $\ln|x|=-at+c$, i.e. $x=\lambda e^{-at}$. $x(0)=2$ gives $x=2e^{-at}$ ...(1)
questions.correction_note: PDF writes 'y(0)=1 therefore mu = e^{-bt}' (a slip: it should be mu = 1, so y = e^{-bt}); the later steps use y = e^{-bt} correctly. Fixed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Look at the ratio $r=\frac xy$: it obeys $\frac{r'}r=b-a$, a constant, so $r=2\,e^{(b-a)t}$ - the values of $a,b$ are never needed separately.

useful_results: For $x'=-ax$ and $y'=-by$, the ratio $\frac xy$ is exponential with rate $b-a$: only the difference $b-a$ matters in any question comparing $x$ and $y$.
Meeting time: $r(t)=r(0)\left(\frac{r(1)}{r(0)}\right)^t=1$ gives $t=\frac{\ln(1/r(0))}{\ln(r(1)/r(0))}$; here $r(0)=2$, $r(1)=\frac32$ give $t=\frac{\ln2}{\ln(4/3)}$.

questions.question: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution curve of the differential equation $(x^2-4)\,dy-(y^2-3y)\,dx=0$, $x>2$, $y(4)=\frac32$ and the slope of the curve is never zero, then the value of $y(10)$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Separate with partial fractions; the slope never being zero keeps $y$ between the constant solutions $0$ and $3$, which fixes the modulus signs.
solution: $\frac1{y(y-3)}=\frac13\left(\frac1{y-3}-\frac1y\right)$, so the left side integrates to $\frac13\left(\ln|y-3|-\ln|y|\right)$; the right side is $\frac14\ln\left|\frac{x-2}{x+2}\right|$.
The slope $y'=\frac{y(y-3)}{x^2-4}$ is never zero, so $y$ never equals $0$ or $3$; since $y(4)=\frac32\in(0,3)$, $y\in(0,3)$ throughout.

alternate_solutions.idea: The Möbius variable $w=\frac{y-3}{y}$ makes the equation linear: $w'=\frac{3w}{x^2-4}$, so the ratio $\frac{w(10)}{w(4)}$ is a pure power.

useful_results: For $y'=f(x)\,y(y-a)$ the substitution $w=\frac{y-a}{y}$ gives $w'=a\,f(x)\,w$: the ratio $\frac{y-a}{y}$ is an exponential of $a\int f$.

A solution of $y'=g(x)h(y)$ cannot cross a constant solution $y=c$ with $h(c)=0$; 'slope never zero' means exactly this, and tells you which side the curve lives on (so the signs of $|y-3|$, $|y|$ are fixed).
$\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}=\frac1{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+C$.

questions.question: A function $y=f(x)$ satisfies $f(x)\sin2x+\sin x-(1+\cos^2x)f'(x)=0$ with condition $f(0)=0$. Then, $f\left(\frac\pi2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The integrating factor is $1+\cos^2x$ because $\frac{d}{dx}(1+\cos^2x)=-\sin2x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The equation says $\frac{d}{dx}\left[f(x)(1+\cos^2x)\right]=\sin x$: integrate from $0$ to $\frac\pi2$ and never find $f$ itself.

useful_results: If $P=-\frac{g'}{g}$ then the integrating factor is $g$, and $g\,y'-g'y\ldots$: precisely, $\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot g\right)=g\,y'+g'y$; here $g=1+\cos^2x$, $g'=-\sin2x$ and the equation says $\left(f\cdot g\right)'=\sin x$.
Recognise $\sin2x=-\frac{d}{dx}(\cos^2x)=-\frac{d}{dx}(1+\cos^2x)$: the coefficient is a logarithmic derivative.
Check: $f(x)=\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos^2x}$ gives $f(0)=0$ and $f\left(\frac\pi2\right)=1$.

questions.question: If $\sin\left(\frac yx\right)=\log_e|x|+\frac\alpha2$ is the solution of the differential equation $x\cos\left(\frac yx\right)\frac{dy}{dx}=y\cos\left(\frac yx\right)+x$ and $y(1)=\frac\pi3$, then $\alpha^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $\frac yx=t$: the equation becomes $\cos t\,dt=\frac{dx}{x}$.
solution: The equation is $x\cos\frac yx\frac{dy}{dx}-y\cos\frac yx=x$, i.e. $\cos\frac yx\left(x\frac{dy}{dx}-y\right)=x$.
The solution is $\sin\frac yx=\ln|x|+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$; comparing with $\ln|x|+\frac\alpha2$: $\alpha=\sqrt3$, so $\alpha^2=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The solution form is given, so no integration is needed: just impose $y(1)=\frac\pi3$ on $\sin\frac yx=\ln|x|+\frac\alpha2$.
solution: The problem states that $\sin\frac yx=\ln|x|+\frac\alpha2$ is the solution with $y(1)=\frac\pi3$.
Check that the form is consistent: differentiating $\sin\frac yx=\ln x+c$ gives $\cos\frac yx\cdot\frac{xy'-y}{x^2}=\frac1x$, which is the given equation. Hence $\alpha^2=3$.

useful_results: When a question gives the form of the solution with an unknown constant, use the initial condition directly; differentiate the form once to confirm it solves the equation.
$x\,y'-y=x^2\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac yx\right)$: the combination $xy'-y$ signals $t=\frac yx$.
Homogeneous-type equations $F\left(\frac yx\right)(xy'-y)=x$ reduce to $F(t)\,dt=\frac{dx}{x}$.

concepts: Exact differentials and integration by parts
questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\sec x\,dy+\{2(1-x)\tan x+x(2-x)\}dx=0$ such that $y(0)=2$. Then $y(2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: After multiplying by $\cos x$ the integrand is $2(x-1)\sin x+(x^2-2x)\cos x=\frac{d}{dx}\left[(x^2-2x)\sin x\right]$.
solution: $\int(x^2-2x)\cos x\,dx=(x^2-2x)\sin x+(2x-2)\cos x-2\sin x$ (by parts twice).
Add: $y=-2(x-1)\cos x+2\sin x+(x^2-2x)\sin x+(2x-2)\cos x-2\sin x+c=(x^2-2x)\sin x+c$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's last line 'y(2) = 2(1+sin 2) - 2 sin 2 = 2' does not follow from its own antiderivative (at x = 2 its terms give 2(-cos 2 + sin 2) + (2 cos 2 - 2 sin 2) + C = C). The final value 2 is right; the working was replaced by the simplified antiderivative (x^2-2x) sin x + C.

alternate_solutions.idea: Spot the antiderivative instead of integrating by parts: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[(x^2-2x)\sin x\right]=(2x-2)\sin x+(x^2-2x)\cos x$, which is the integrand... up to the factor 2 in the first term - check carefully.
solution: Let $g(x)=(x^2-2x)\sin x$. Then $g'(x)=(2x-2)\sin x+(x^2-2x)\cos x=2(x-1)\sin x+(x^2-2x)\cos x$.
This is exactly the integrand of $dy=\left[2(x-1)\sin x+(x^2-2x)\cos x\right]dx$, so $dy=dg$ and $y=(x^2-2x)\sin x+C$.
$y(0)=2$ gives $C=2$. At $x=2$ the factor $x^2-2x=0$, so $y(2)=C=2$ with no further computation.

useful_results: If the right side is $\left[f'(x)\,g(x)+f(x)\,g'(x)\right]$, it is the exact derivative of $f(x)g(x)$ - test the product $(x^2-2x)\sin x$ before integrating by parts.
$\int p(x)\sin x\,dx$ and $\int p(x)\cos x\,dx$ for polynomial $p$: the answer has the form $A(x)\sin x+B(x)\cos x$ with polynomials $A,B$ of the same degree.
$x^2-2x=x(x-2)$ vanishes at $x=0,2$: that is why $y(0)=y(2)$ here.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(\tan x)+y}{\sin x(\sec x-\sin x\tan x)}$, $x\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$ satisfying the condition $y\left(\frac\pi4\right)=2$. Then $y\left(\frac\pi3\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Simplify the denominator to $\sin x\cos x$ times $\sec x\ldots$: the equation becomes $y'-2\csc2x\,y=\sec^2x$ with integrating factor $\cot x$.
solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by $\cos x$: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\sin x+y\cos x}{\sin x\left(1-\sin^2x\right)}=\frac{\sin x+y\cos x}{\sin x\cos^2x}$.

Integrating factor: $e^{-\int2\csc2x\,dx}$. With $2x=t$: $\int2\csc2x\,dx=\int\csc t\,dt=\ln\left|\tan\frac t2\right|=\ln|\tan x|$, so $\text{I.F.}=\frac1{|\tan x|}=\cot x$ for $x\in\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)$.
$y\cot x=\int\sec^2x\cot x\,dx=\int\frac{\sec^2x}{\tan x}dx$. Put $\tan x=t$: $\int\frac{dt}{t}=\ln t+c$.
So $y\cot x=\ln\tan x+c$, i.e. $y=\tan x\left(\ln\tan x+c\right)$.
useful_results: $\int\csc t\,dt=\ln\left|\tan\frac t2\right|+C$, hence $\int2\csc2x\,dx=\ln|\tan x|+C$ (since $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$ gives $2\csc2x=\frac{1}{\sin x\cos x}=\frac{\sec^2x}{\tan x}$).
Simplify trigonometric coefficients before choosing a method: $\sec x-\sin x\tan x=\frac{1-\sin^2x}{\cos x}=\cos x$.
$y=\tan x\cdot u$ with $u'=\frac{\sec^2x}{\tan x}$: the homogeneous solution of $y'=2\csc2x\,y$ is $\tan x$.

questions.question: The solution curve of the differential equation $y\frac{dx}{dy}=x\left(\log_ex-\log_ey+1\right)$, $x>0,y>0$ passing through the point $(e,1)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Put $x=vy$: the equation separates as $\frac{dv}{v\ln v}=\frac{dy}{y}$.
solution: $\ln(\ln v)=\ln y+\ln c$, so $\ln v=cy$, i.e. $\ln\frac xy=cy$.
The curve passes through $(e,1)$: $\ln e=c\cdot1$, so $c=1$ and $\ln\frac xy=y$.
Since $y>0$, this is $y=\ln\frac xy$, i.e. $\left|\ln\frac xy\right|=y$, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Test the options: each is a relation $\ln\frac xy=g(y)$; differentiate it with respect to $y$ and compare with the equation.
solution: The equation says $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac xy\left(\ln\frac xy+1\right)$. Each option gives $\ln\frac xy=g(y)$ ($=y^2$, $y$, or $\frac{y+1}2$ near $(e,1)$ where $\ln\frac xy=1>0$).
From $\ln x-\ln y=g(y)$: $\frac1x\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac1y+g'(y)$, so $\frac{dx}{dy}=x\left(\frac1y+g'\right)$. The equation requires $\frac1y+g'=\frac{g+1}{y}$, i.e. $g'=\frac gy$, i.e. $y\,g'=g$.
Hence the curve is (D) $\ln\frac xy=y$ (indeed $y\,g'=g$ forces $g=cy$).

useful_results: If $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac xyF\left(\frac xy\right)$ then $x=vy$ gives $y\,v'=v\left(F(v)-1\right)$; here $F=\ln v+1$ so $\frac{dv}{v\ln v}=\frac{dy}{y}$ and $\ln v=cy$.
$\int\frac{dv}{v\ln v}=\ln|\ln v|+C$ (put $\ln v=u$).
For multiple-choice implicit relations: eliminate by the given point first, then by differentiating the survivors.

questions.question: The temperature $T(t)$ of a body at time $t=0$ is $160^\circ$F and it decreases continuously as per the differential equation $\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-80)$, where $k$ is a positive constant. If $T(15)=120^\circ$F, then $T(45)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The excess $T-80$ decays exponentially; $T(15)-80$ is half of $T(0)-80$, so it halves every 15 units.

alternate_solutions.idea: Newton's law: the excess temperature over $80^\circ$ shrinks by the same factor in equal time intervals, so it halves every 15 minutes.
solution: Excess at $t=0$: $160-80=80$. At $t=15$: $120-80=40$: a factor $\frac12$ in $15$ units.
Equal intervals give equal factors (exponential decay): at $t=30$ the excess is $20$, at $t=45$ it is $10$.

useful_results: For $T'=-k(T-T_0)$: $T-T_0$ is multiplied by the same factor over every equal time interval - it is a geometric progression in time.
Half-life of the excess: $t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{k}$; here $15$ units.
$T(t)=T_0+(T(0)-T_0)\left(\frac{T(\tau)-T_0}{T(0)-T_0}\right)^{t/\tau}$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x(x+y)^3-x(x+y)-1$, $y(0)=1$. Then $\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}+y\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\right)^2$ equals:
questions.key_idea: $t=x+y$ separates the equation to $\frac{dt}{t(2t^2-1)}=x\,dx$; then $z=t^2$ turns it into a standard partial fraction.
solution: At $x=\frac1{\sqrt2}$ ($x^2=\frac12$): $\frac{z-\frac12}{z}=\frac{\sqrt e}{2}$, i.e. $1-\frac1{2z}=\frac{\sqrt e}2$, so $\frac1{2z}=\frac{2-\sqrt e}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $u=\frac1{(x+y)^2}$: the equation $t'=xt(2t^2-1)$ becomes the linear equation $u'-2xu=-4x$, with the obvious particular solution $u=2$.
solution: So $u'=2xu-4x$, a linear equation with the particular solution $u=2$ (check: $0=4x-4x$); the complementary solution is $Ce^{x^2}$. Hence $u=2+Ce^{x^2}$.

useful_results: If $y'=f(x,\,x+y)$ (the dependence on $y$ only through $x+y$), put $t=x+y$: $t'=1+f$. Similarly for $ax+by$.
For $t'=g(x)\left(at^3+bt\right)$ (Bernoulli in $t$ with exponent 3), $u=t^{-2}$ gives the linear equation $u'=-2g(x)\left(a+bu\right)$.
$\int\frac{dz}{z(2z-1)}=\ln\left|\frac{2z-1}{z}\right|+C$.

questions.question: Let $\alpha$ be a non-zero real number. Suppose $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is a differentiable function such that $f(0)=2$ and $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=1$. If $f'(x)=\alpha f(x)+3$, for all $x\in\mathbb R$, then $f(-\log_e2)$ is equal to:
questions.answer: Bonus (the data are inconsistent: no such function exists)
questions.key_idea: Solving gives $f=-\frac3\alpha+Ce^{\alpha x}$; the two conditions at $0$ and at $-\infty$ cannot both hold for any real non-zero $\alpha$.
solution: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\alpha y+3$, so $\int\frac{dy}{\alpha y+3}=\int dx$ and $\frac1\alpha\ln|\alpha y+3|=x+C$, i.e. $\alpha y+3=ce^{\alpha x}$ (with $c$ a real constant).
So $f(x)=-\frac3\alpha+\frac c\alpha e^{\alpha x}$, with $f(0)=2$ giving $\frac c\alpha=2+\frac3\alpha$.
If $\alpha>0$: $e^{\alpha x}\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$, so $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f=-\frac3\alpha$. Setting this equal to $1$ gives $\alpha=-3$, which contradicts $\alpha>0$.
If $\alpha<0$: $e^{\alpha x}\to\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$, so the limit is finite only if $c=0$; then $f\equiv-\frac3\alpha=f(0)=2$ and the limit is $2\ne1$ - again a contradiction.
So no real $\alpha\ne0$ makes both conditions true: the data contradict each other, and the key lists this as Bonus.

alternate_solutions.idea: If $f\to1$ at $-\infty$ then $f'\to0$, which forces $\alpha=-3$; but then the explicit solution $1+e^{-3x}$ blows up at $-\infty$.
solution: If $f(x)\to1$ as $x\to-\infty$, then $f'(x)=\alpha f(x)+3\to\alpha+3$. A bounded function with a limiting derivative $L\ne0$ would be unbounded, so $\alpha+3=0$, i.e. $\alpha=-3$.
So the conditions cannot all hold: the question has no valid answer (Bonus). (The tempting answer $f(-\ln2)=1+e^{3\ln2}=9$ comes from ignoring the limit condition.)

useful_results: For $f'=\alpha f+3$ the only equilibrium is $f=-\frac3\alpha$; solutions are $f=-\frac3\alpha+Ce^{\alpha x}$ and approach the equilibrium as $x\to-\infty$ iff $\alpha>0$ (as $x\to+\infty$ iff $\alpha<0$).
If $f$ has a finite limit at $\pm\infty$ and $f'$ has a limit there, then that limit of $f'$ is $0$ (else $f$ is unbounded) - this identifies the equilibrium: $\alpha L+3=0$.
Always check that all given conditions are mutually consistent before computing the asked value.

questions.question: If the solution of the differential equation $(2x+3y-2)\,dx+(4x+6y-7)\,dy=0$, $y(0)=3$, is $\alpha x+\beta y+3\log_e|2x+3y-\gamma|=6$, then $\alpha+2\beta+3\gamma$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Put $t=2x+3y$ (parallel-line type): the equation separates; $\frac{2t-7}{t-8}=2+\frac9{t-8}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF working stops at '2(2x+3y)+9|2x+3y-8| = x + c' (the logarithm sign is missing from the printed line) and never applies y(0)=3 or compares with the given form; those steps were completed. Answer 29 is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ without integrating: differentiate the claimed first integral and require it to be proportional to the given 1-form.
solution: Compare the $dx$ coefficients: $\alpha t+(6-\alpha\gamma)=\lambda(t-2)$, so $\lambda=\alpha$ and $6-\alpha\gamma=-2\alpha$.
Compare the $dy$ coefficients: $\beta t+(9-\beta\gamma)=\alpha(2t-7)$, so $\beta=2\alpha$ and $9-\beta\gamma=-7\alpha$, i.e. $9-2\alpha\gamma=-7\alpha$.
From $\alpha\gamma=6+2\alpha$: $9-12-4\alpha=-7\alpha$, so $\alpha=1,\ \beta=2,\ \gamma=8$. Check the constant: at $(0,3)$, $0+6+3\ln|9-8|=6$ ✓.

useful_results: For $(a_1x+b_1y+c_1)dx+(a_2x+b_2y+c_2)dy=0$ with $\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{b_1}{b_2}$ (parallel lines), put $t=a_1x+b_1y$ - the equation becomes separable in $t$ and $x$.
For a rational integrand $\frac{pt+q}{t-r}$: divide first, $\frac{pt+q}{t-r}=p+\frac{q+pr}{t-r}$ (here $2+\frac{9}{t-8}$).
A prescribed form of the answer can be matched by differentiating it - the unknown coefficients are fixed by comparing the differential with the original equation.

questions.question: If the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y-2}{x-y}$ passing through the point $(2,1)$ is $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y-1}{x-1}\right)-\frac1\beta\log_e\left(\alpha+\left(\frac{y-1}{x-1}\right)^2\right)=\log_e|x-1|$, then $5\beta+\alpha$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Shift the origin to the intersection $(1,1)$ of $x+y-2=0$ and $x-y=0$; the equation becomes homogeneous.
solution: The lines $x+y-2=0$ and $x-y=0$ meet at $(1,1)$. Put $x=X+1,\ y=Y+1$: $\frac{dY}{dX}=\frac{X+Y}{X-Y}$.
The curve passes through $(2,1)$: $X=1,\ t=0$, so $0=0-0+C$ and $C=0$.
So $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{y-1}{x-1}\right)-\frac12\ln\left(1+\left(\frac{y-1}{x-1}\right)^2\right)=\ln|x-1|$. Comparing with the given form: $\alpha=1,\ \beta=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In polar coordinates about $(1,1)$ the equation $X\,dY-Y\,dX=X\,dX+Y\,dY$ reads $r^2d\theta=r\,dr$: a logarithmic spiral $r=Ce^{\theta}$.
solution: With $X=x-1,\ Y=y-1$, the equation $(X-Y)\,dY=(X+Y)\,dX$ rearranges to $X\,dY-Y\,dX=X\,dX+Y\,dY$.
So $\ln|X|+\frac12\ln(1+t^2)=\tan^{-1}t+C$; the point $(2,1)$ ($X=1,t=0$) gives $C=0$. This is the given form with $\alpha=1$, $\beta=2$, so $5\beta+\alpha=11$.

useful_results: For $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}$ with non-parallel lines, shift the origin to their intersection; the equation becomes homogeneous.
$X\,dY-Y\,dX=r^2d\theta$ and $X\,dX+Y\,dY=r\,dr$: equations built from these two combinations are separable in polar form (spirals).
$\int\frac{1-t}{1+t^2}dt=\tan^{-1}t-\frac12\ln(1+t^2)+C$.

questions.question: If the solution curve $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $(1+y^2)(1+\log_ex)\,dx+x\,dy=0$, $x>0$ passes through the point $(1,1)$ and $y(e)=\frac{\alpha-\tan\left(\frac32\right)}{\beta+\tan\left(\frac32\right)}$, then $\alpha+2\beta$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: Separate: $\frac{1+\ln x}{x}dx=-\frac{dy}{1+y^2}$, then use $\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
useful_results: $\tan\left(\frac\pi4-\theta\right)=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$ and $\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\theta\right)=\frac{1+\tan\theta}{1-\tan\theta}$.
$\int\frac{1+\ln x}{x}dx=\frac{(1+\ln x)^2}{2}+C$ (substitute $u=1+\ln x$).
The answer's form is fixed once the angle is written as $\frac\pi4-\theta$: the constants must be read off from the identity, not from numerical values.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{\lim_{r\to x}\left\{\frac{2r^2\left[(f(r))^2-f(x)f(r)\right]}{r^2-x^2}-r^3e^{\frac{f(r)}{r}}\right\}}$ be differentiable in $(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$ and $f(1)=1$. Then the value of $ea$, such that $f(a)=0$, is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The limit is $xf(x)f'(x)-x^3e^{f/x}$ (a difference quotient), so $f^2=xff'-x^3e^{f/x}$, which is homogeneous.
solution: As $r\to x$, $\frac{2r^2f(r)\left(f(r)-f(x)\right)}{(r-x)(r+x)}\to\frac{2x^2f(x)f'(x)}{2x}=xf(x)f'(x)$ (L'Hospital's rule / definition of $f'$), and $r^3e^{f(r)/r}\to x^3e^{f(x)/x}$.
Integrate: $\int ve^{-v}dv=-(v+1)e^{-v}$, so $-(v+1)e^{-v}=x+c_1$, i.e. $(x+c)e^{v}+v+1=0$, i.e. $(x+c)e^{y/x}+\frac yx+1=0$.
useful_results: A limit of the form $\lim_{r\to x}\frac{g(r)-g(x)}{r-x}$ is $g'(x)$; here $\frac{2r^2f(r)\,(f(r)-f(x))}{(r-x)(r+x)}\to\frac{2x^2f(x)}{2x}f'(x)$ - factor the difference of squares first.
A homogeneous equation with $e^{y/x}$: after $y=vx$ the equation becomes $v\,v'=e^v$-type; $\int ve^{-v}dv=-(v+1)e^{-v}+C$.
Since $f$ is a square root it is $\ge0$; the point $f(a)=0$ corresponds to $v=0$, which simplifies the implicit relation at once.

questions.question: Let $Y=Y(X)$ be a curve lying in the first quadrant such that the area enclosed by the line $Y-y=Y'(x)(X-x)$ and the co-ordinate axes, where $(x,y)$ is any point on the curve, is always $\frac{-y^2}{2Y'(x)}+1$, $Y'(x)\ne0$. If $Y(1)=1$, then $12Y(2)$ equals ________.
questions.key_idea: The intercepts of the tangent are $x-\frac y{y'}$ and $y-xy'$; equating the (signed) triangle area to the given expression collapses to $x^2y'-2xy+2=0$.
solution: The tangent $Y-y=y'(X-x)$ meets the $x$-axis at $\left(x-\frac y{y'},0\right)$ and the $y$-axis at $(0,\,y-xy')$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve $x^2y'-2xy+2=0$ as 'particular solution plus homogeneous solution': the homogeneous equation $x^2y'=2xy$ has solutions $Cx^2$ and $y=\frac kx$ is a particular solution.
solution: After the equation $x^2y'-2xy+2=0$ is reached, note the homogeneous equation $x^2y'=2xy$ gives $\frac{y'}{y}=\frac2x$, so $y_h=Cx^2$.

useful_results: Intercepts of the tangent at $(x,y)$ with slope $m$: $x$-intercept $x-\frac ym$, $y$-intercept $y-mx$; the triangle area is $\frac{(y-mx)^2}{2|m|}$.

The product of intercepts is $-\frac{(y-mx)^2}{m}$, so a 'signed' area condition is $-\frac{(y-xm)^2}{2m}=$ given expression; the $y^2$ terms cancel when the right side is $-\frac{y^2}{2m}+\text{const}$, giving a linear equation.
$x^2y'-2xy=-2$ means $\left(\frac{y}{x^2}\right)'=-\frac{2}{x^4}$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\sec^2x\,dx+\left(e^{2y}\tan^2x+\tan x\right)dy=0$, $0<x<\frac\pi2$, $y\left(\frac\pi4\right)=0$. If $y\left(\frac\pi6\right)=\alpha$, then $e^{8\alpha}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: $t=\tan x$ makes it Bernoulli in $t$ ($t'=-t-e^{2y}t^2$); $u=\frac1t$ then gives a linear equation.
questions.correction_note: PDF working stops after 'u e^{-y} = integral of e^{-y} e^{2y} dy' (page break); the integration, the constant c = 0 and the final evaluation e^{8 alpha} = 9 were completed. Answer 9 is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: The combination $s=e^{2y}\tan x$ turns the equation into $ds=s(1-s)\,dy$, which has the constant solution $s=1$ - and the initial point lies on it.
solution: Let $s=e^{2y}\tan x$. Then $ds=e^{2y}\sec^2x\,dx+2s\,dy$, so $e^{2y}\sec^2x\,dx=ds-2s\,dy$, and $e^{4y}\tan^2x+e^{2y}\tan x=s^2+s$.
$s\equiv1$ is a constant solution and at $\left(\frac\pi4,0\right)$: $s=e^0\cdot1=1$. By uniqueness $s=1$ always: $e^{2y}\tan x=1$.

useful_results: If $x$ is easier as the dependent variable, treat the equation as $\frac{dt}{dy}=\ldots$ with $t=\tan x$; $\frac{dt}{dy}=-t-e^{2y}t^2$ is Bernoulli ($n=2$).
When the initial point makes some natural combination equal to a constant solution (here $s=1$), the solution is that constant: check this before integrating.
$e^{8\alpha}=\left(e^{2\alpha}\right)^4$: the answer needs only $e^{2\alpha}=\sqrt3$.

questions.question: If $x=x(t)$ is the solution of the differential equation $(t+1)\,dx=\left(2x+(t+1)^4\right)dt$, $x(0)=2$, then $x(1)$ equals ________.
questions.key_idea: The equation is linear in $x$ with integrating factor $\frac1{(t+1)^2}$.
useful_results: $\frac{dx}{dt}-\frac{n}{t+1}x=g(t)$ has integrating factor $(t+1)^{-n}$, and $\left(\frac{x}{(t+1)^n}\right)'=\frac{g}{(t+1)^n}$ - the quotient $\frac{x}{(t+1)^2}$ is the natural variable.
Check: $x(t)=\left(\frac{t^2}{2}+t+2\right)(t+1)^2$ gives $x(0)=2$ and $x(1)=14$.

questions.question: If $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1+x-y^2}{y}$, $x(1)=1$, then $5x(2)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Linear in $x$ with integrating factor $\frac1y$.
useful_results: $\frac{dx}{dy}-\frac xy=g(y)$ gives $\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac xy\right)=\frac{g(y)}{y}$.
Equivalent form: $y\,dx-x\,dy=y^2\,d\left(\frac xy\right)$, so the equation reads $d\left(\frac xy\right)=\frac{1-y^2}{y^2}dy$.
Check: $x=-1-y^2+3y$ gives $x(1)=1$ and $x(2)=1$.

questions.question: If the solution $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $(x^4+2x^3+3x^2+2x+2)\,dy-(2x^2+2x+3)\,dx=0$ satisfies $y(-1)=-\frac\pi4$, then $y(0)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Factor $x^4+2x^3+3x^2+2x+2=(x^2+1)(x^2+2x+2)$; the integrand splits as $\frac1{x^2+1}+\frac1{(x+1)^2+1}$.
useful_results: Spotting the partial-fraction split: if $N=D_1+D_2$ for $D=D_1D_2$ then $\frac ND=\frac1{D_1}\cdot\ldots$ precisely $\frac{D_1+D_2}{D_1D_2}=\frac1{D_1}+\frac1{D_2}$; here $D_1=x^2+1$, $D_2=x^2+2x+2$ and $D_1+D_2=2x^2+2x+3$.
$\int\frac{dx}{(x+a)^2+b^2}=\frac1b\tan^{-1}\frac{x+a}b+C$.
Factorisation tip: $x^4+2x^3+3x^2+2x+2$ at $x=\pm i$ vanishes, so $(x^2+1)$ is a factor.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(x^2+4)^2dy+(2x^3y+8xy-2)\,dx=0$. If $y(0)=0$, then $y(2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $2x^3y+8xy=2xy(x^2+4)$, so the equation is linear with integrating factor $x^2+4$.
useful_results: If $P=\frac{f'}{f}$ the integrating factor is $f$; here $P=\frac{2x}{x^2+4}$, $f=x^2+4$, and the equation says $\left((x^2+4)y\right)'=\frac{2}{x^2+4}$.
$\int\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa+C$, so $\int\frac2{x^2+4}dx=\tan^{-1}\frac x2+C$.
Factor the coefficient before choosing a method: $2x^3y+8xy=2xy(x^2+4)$.

questions.question: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=\sin(2x)$, $y(0)=\frac34$, then $y\left(\frac\pi8\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Integrating factor $e^{2x}$; $\int e^{2x}\sin2x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}}8(2\sin2x-2\cos2x)$, and at $x=\frac\pi8$ the sine and cosine are equal.
solution: By the formula $\int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx-b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}$ with $a=b=2$: $\int e^{2x}\sin2x\,dx=\frac{e^{2x}}{8}(2\sin2x-2\cos2x)$.
At $x=\frac\pi8$: $\sin\frac\pi4=\cos\frac\pi4$, so the bracket vanishes and $y\left(\frac\pi8\right)=e^{-\pi/4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Undetermined coefficients: a trigonometric particular solution plus the decaying complementary solution $Ce^{-2x}$ - no integration by parts.
solution: Match with $\sin2x$: $2A-2B=1$ and $2A+2B=0$, so $A=\frac14,\ B=-\frac14$ and $y_p=\frac14(\sin2x-\cos2x)$.
The complementary solution of $y'+2y=0$ is $Ce^{-2x}$, so $y=\frac14(\sin2x-\cos2x)+Ce^{-2x}$.

useful_results: For $y'+ky=\sin\omega x$ ($k>0$): $y_p=\frac{k\sin\omega x-\omega\cos\omega x}{k^2+\omega^2}$ and $y=y_p+Ce^{-kx}$; the transient is $Ce^{-kx}$.
$y_p=\frac14(\sin2x-\cos2x)=\frac{\sqrt2}4\sin\left(2x-\frac\pi4\right)$ vanishes at $x=\frac\pi8$, which is why $y\left(\frac\pi8\right)=C\,e^{-\pi/4}$.
$\int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx-b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C$ and $\int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}(a\cos bx+b\sin bx)}{a^2+b^2}+C$.

questions.question: The differential equation of the family of circles passing through the origin and having centre at the line $y=x$ is:
questions.key_idea: The family has one parameter, $x^2+y^2+gx+gy=0$; eliminate $g$ by differentiating once.
solution: The centre is $\left(-\frac g2,-\frac g2\right)$ on $y=x$ and the circle passes through the origin, so $C:\ x^2+y^2+gx+gy=0$ ...(1).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the family as $\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}=-g$: a constant. Differentiate the quotient and set it to zero - $g$ never has to be solved for.

useful_results: Elimination of the arbitrary constant: if the family is $F(x,y)=c$, the differential equation is $dF=0$; when the constant appears as a ratio ($\frac{x^2+y^2}{x+y}=-g$) differentiate the ratio.
Number of arbitrary constants = order of the equation: circles through the origin with centre on $y=x$ have one parameter, so a first-order equation.
Circle through the origin: $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy=0$; centre on $y=x$ forces $g=f$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(2x\log_ex)\frac{dy}{dx}+2y=\frac3x\log_ex$, $x>0$ and $y(e^{-1})=0$. Then, $y(e)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Dividing by $2x$ the left side becomes $\frac{d}{dx}(y\ln x)$, so the equation integrates at once.
solution: Divide the equation by $2x$: $\ln x\,\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac yx=\frac{3\ln x}{2x^2}$.
The left side is $\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\ln x\right)$ (equivalently the integrating factor of $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x\ln x}=\frac3{2x^2}$ is $\ln x$).
$y(e^{-1})=0$: $\ln e^{-1}=-1$, so the left side is $0$ and $-\frac{3(-1+1)}{2/e}+C=0$ gives $C=0$.
Remark: this solution blows up at $x=1$ (where $\ln x=0$), so the question takes the same constant $C=0$ on both sides of $x=1$, as the key does.
questions.correction_note: The solution printed in the PDF under Q49 is a copy of Q50's solution ((1+x^2)y' + y = e^{tan^-1 x}), so it does not belong to this question. A complete solution was written. Answer B (-3/e) agrees with the key.
useful_results: If the coefficients are $P=\frac{f'}{f}$ the integrating factor is $f$; here $\frac1{x\ln x}$ is not of that form but $\ln x\,y'+\frac{y}{x}=(y\ln x)'$ after dividing by $2x$.
$\int\frac{\ln x}{x^2}dx=-\frac{\ln x+1}{x}+C$ (by parts or differentiate $-\frac{\ln x+1}x$).
The equation is singular at $x=1$ (the coefficient of $y'$ vanishes): a solution through $(e^{-1},0)$ is a solution on $(0,1)$ only; extending to $x>1$ needs a convention.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(1+x^2)\frac{dy}{dx}+y=e^{\tan^{-1}x}$, $y(1)=0$. Then $y(0)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Put $t=\tan^{-1}x$ so that $(1+x^2)\frac{d}{dx}=\frac{d}{dt}$: the equation becomes $\frac{dy}{dt}+y=e^t$.
solution: The equation becomes $\frac{dy}{dt}+y=e^t$, linear with integrating factor $e^{\int dt}=e^t$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes 'y . tan^-1 x = e^{2 tan^-1 x}/2 - e^{pi/2}/2' (the left side should be y . e^{tan^-1 x}); the final value is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: In the variable $t=\tan^{-1}x$ the equation $y'+y=e^t$ has the obvious particular solution $\frac12e^t$ (since $\frac12e^t+\frac12e^t=e^t$).

useful_results: When the coefficient of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is $1+x^2$, $t=\tan^{-1}x$ gives $(1+x^2)\frac{d}{dx}=\frac d{dt}$: the equation becomes constant-coefficient.
For $y'+y=e^{kt}$ ($k\neq-1$): $y=\frac{e^{kt}}{k+1}+Ce^{-t}$.
Check: $y(0)=\frac12\left(1-e^{\pi/2}\right)<0$ and $y(1)=0$.

questions.question: Suppose the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{(2+\alpha)x-\beta y+2}{\beta x-2\alpha y-(\beta\gamma-4\alpha)}$ represents a circle passing through origin. Then the radius of this circle is:
questions.key_idea: $\beta(x\,dy+y\,dx)=\beta\,d(xy)$ gives an $xy$ term, so a circle needs $\beta=0$; then equal $x^2,y^2$ coefficients give $\alpha=2$.
solution: A circle has no $xy$ term, so $\beta=0$: $\frac{(2+\alpha)}{2}x^2+\alpha y^2+2x-4\alpha y+c=0$.
Equal coefficients of $x^2$ and $y^2$: $\frac{2+\alpha}{2}=\alpha$, so $\alpha=2$. The equation is $2x^2+2y^2+2x-8y+c=0$.
It passes through the origin, so $c=0$: $x^2+y^2+x-4y=0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF reads the printed '(beta gamma - 4 alpha)' as '(beta y - 4 alpha)' in its first line (so the y-coefficient becomes -(2 alpha + beta)) and omits the +2x on the right before the next line, though it reappears later. With beta = 0 (forced by the absence of an xy term) both readings give the same circle, so the answer is unchanged; the working above follows the printed gamma.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare slopes: a circle through the origin $x^2+y^2+px+qy=0$ has $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{2x+p}{2y+q}$; match it with the given quotient coefficient by coefficient - no integration.
solution: Require $-(2x+p)=\lambda\left((2+\alpha)x-\beta y+2\right)$ and $2y+q=\lambda\left(\beta x-2\alpha y-\beta\gamma+4\alpha\right)$ for a function (constant) $\lambda$.
The $y$-term of the first: $0=-\lambda\beta$, so $\beta=0$. Then the $y$-coefficient of the second: $2=-2\alpha\lambda$, so $\lambda=-\frac1\alpha$.
Constants: $-p=2\lambda=-1$, so $p=1$; $q=\lambda(4\alpha)=-4$. The circle is $x^2+y^2+x-4y=0$ (through the origin) with radius $\sqrt{\frac14+4}=\frac{\sqrt{17}}2$.

useful_results: $y\,dx+x\,dy=d(xy)$ is the only source of an $xy$ term when integrating a first-order equation: a circle (no $xy$ term) therefore needs the coefficient $\beta$ of this term to vanish.
Circle $\Leftrightarrow$ equal coefficients of $x^2$ and $y^2$ and no $xy$ term; radius $\sqrt{g^2+f^2-c}$ for $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$.
The slope of $x^2+y^2+px+qy=0$ is $-\frac{2x+p}{2y+q}$: comparing coefficients is a quick way to identify the circle.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(1+y^2)e^{\tan x}dx+\cos^2x\,(1+e^{2\tan x})\,dy=0$, $y(0)=1$. Then $y\left(\frac\pi4\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $t=e^{\tan x}$: $dt=e^{\tan x}\sec^2x\,dx$, giving $\tan^{-1}y+\tan^{-1}\left(e^{\tan x}\right)=C$.
solution: Let $e^{\tan x}=t$, so $e^{\tan x}\sec^2x\,dx=dt$ and the right side is $-\frac{dt}{1+t^2}$.
Taking tangent: $\frac{y+e}{1-ye}=\tan\frac\pi2$ is infinite, so $1-ye=0$ and $y=\frac1e$.
useful_results: $\tan^{-1}a+\tan^{-1}b=\frac\pi2$ (for $a,b>0$) iff $ab=1$; so $\tan^{-1}y+\tan^{-1}e=\frac\pi2$ gives $y=\frac1e$ immediately.
If the equation has the form $f(y)\,dy=g(x)\,dx$ with $g=h'(x)\,k(h(x))$, put $t=h(x)$ (here $h=e^{\tan x}$).
$\frac{d}{dx}e^{\tan x}=e^{\tan x}\sec^2x$.

questions.question: Let $f(x)$ be a positive function such that the area bounded by $y=f(x)$, $y=0$ from $x=0$ to $x=a>0$ is $e^{-a}+4a^2+a-1$. Then the differential equation, whose general solution is $y=c_1f(x)+c_2$, where $c_1$ and $c_2$ are arbitrary constants, is:
questions.key_idea: Differentiate the area w.r.t. $a$ to get $f$, then eliminate $c_1,c_2$ with two derivatives.
useful_results: If $\int_0^af=F(a)$ then $f=F'$ (Fundamental Theorem): areas under a curve given as a function of the upper limit determine the curve.
A family $y=c_1f(x)+c_2$ with two constants has the second-order equation $\frac{y''}{y'}=\frac{f''}{f'}$.
Positivity of $f$: $f(x)=8x+1-e^{-x}>0$ for $x>0$ since $f(0)=0$ and $f'=8+e^{-x}>0$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\sec y\frac{dy}{dx}+2x\sin y=x^3\cos y$, $y(1)=0$. Then $y\left(\sqrt3\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Multiply by $\sec y$: $\sec^2y\,y'+2x\tan y=x^3$, so $z=\tan y$ makes it linear.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess a polynomial particular solution of $z'+2xz=x^3$: $z=\frac{x^2-1}{2}$ works, and the complementary solution $Ce^{-x^2}$ is killed by the condition.

useful_results: A term $\sec^2y\,y'$ (derivative of $\tan y$) or $\cos y\,y'$ (derivative of $\sin y$) signals the substitution $z=\tan y$ or $z=\sin y$; multiply the equation by $\sec y$ or $\sec^2y$ to expose it.
For $z'+2xz=x^n$ with $n$ odd the equation has a polynomial particular solution.

questions.question: The solution curve, of the differential equation $2y\frac{dy}{dx}+3=5\frac{dy}{dx}$, passing through the point $(0,1)$ is a conic, whose vertex lies on the line:
questions.key_idea: Integrate directly: $y^2+3x=5y+c$, a parabola with horizontal axis.

alternate_solutions.idea: The vertex is where the tangent is vertical, i.e. $\frac{dx}{dy}=0$: read it off the equation without completing the square.
solution: $\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{5-2y}{3}$: the parabola has a horizontal axis and its vertex is where $\frac{dx}{dy}=0$, i.e. $y=\frac52$.

useful_results: A parabola $x=ay^2+by+c$ has its vertex where $\frac{dx}{dy}=0$, i.e. $y=-\frac{b}{2a}$; similarly for $y=ax^2+\ldots$ use $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$.
If the equation contains only $y\,dy$, $dx$ and $dy$ terms it is exact: integrate term by term.
$(y-k)^2=4a'(x-h)$ has vertex $(h,k)$; here $4a'=-3$.

questions.question: The solution of the differential equation $(x^2+y^2)\,dx-5xy\,dy=0$, $y(1)=0$, is:
questions.key_idea: Homogeneous: $y=vx$ gives $\frac{5v\,dv}{1-4v^2}=\frac{dx}{x}$ and a logarithm.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $t=y^2$: the equation is linear in $t$ with integrating factor $x^{-2/5}$ - and it gives the sign of $x^2-4y^2$ for free.
solution: Raise to the fifth power: $(x^2-4y^2)^5=x^2$, i.e. $|x^2-4y^2|^5=x^2$, option (A).

useful_results: For $y\,y'=\frac{x^2+y^2}{kx}$ ($k=5$) the substitution $t=y^2$ gives the linear equation $t'-\frac{2}{kx}t=\frac2k x$; the integrating factor is $x^{-2/k}$.
$\int\frac{5v}{1-4v^2}dv=-\frac58\ln|1-4v^2|+C$ (the numerator is a multiple of the derivative of $1-4v^2$).

questions.question: Let $\int_0^x\sqrt{1-(y'(t))^2}\,dt=\int_0^xy(t)\,dt$, $0\le x\le3$, $y\ge0$, $y(0)=0$. Then at $x=2$, $y''+y+1$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Differentiate both sides to get $\sqrt{1-y'^2}=y$, i.e. $y'^2+y^2=1$; with $y(0)=0,\ y\ge0$ the solution is $y=\sin x$.
solution: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: $\sqrt{1-(y'(x))^2}=y(x)$.
$y(0)=0$ gives $c=0$. Since $y\ge0$ we need $\sin^{-1}y=x$ (the other branch gives $y=-\sin x<0$ for $x>0$), so $y=\sin x$ - which is $\ge0$ on $[0,3]$ because $3<\pi$.

Remark: the equation $y'^2=1-y^2$ also has the constant solution $y=1$, so gluing $y=\sin x$ on $[0,\frac\pi2]$ to $y=1$ is another solution (it would give $2$ at $x=2$); the key uses $y=\sin x$ throughout.

alternate_solutions.idea: Don't solve at all: differentiating $y'^2+y^2=1$ gives $y'(y''+y)=0$, so $y''+y=0$ wherever $y'\ne0$.
solution: At $x=2$ the solution is $y=\sin x$ with $y'(2)=\cos2\ne0$, so the quantity is $1$.

useful_results: An integral equation $\int_0^xg=\int_0^xh$ for all $x$ holds iff $g=h$ (differentiate), the starting value being automatic.
$y'^2+y^2=1$ describes the sine curve: $y=\sin(x+\phi)$; differentiating gives $y''=-y$ whenever $y'\ne0$.
The envelope solutions $y=\pm1$ of $y'^2=1-y^2$ are the places where uniqueness fails; the condition $y\ge0$ and $y(0)=0$ selects $\sin x$ near $x=0$.

questions.question: Let the solution $y=y(x)$ of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}-y=1+4\sin x$ satisfy $y(\pi)=1$. Then $y\left(\frac\pi2\right)+10$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Linear with integrating factor $e^{-x}$; the condition $y(\pi)=1$ kills the $e^x$ term.
solution: $\int e^{-x}\sin x\,dx=\frac{e^{-x}}{2}\left(-\sin x-\cos x\right)$, so $ye^{-x}=-e^{-x}+4\cdot\frac{e^{-x}}{2}\left(-\sin x-\cos x\right)+c$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Undetermined coefficients: $y_p=A\sin x+B\cos x+C$, plus $ce^x$.

useful_results: For $y'-y=g(x)$ with $g$ trigonometric/polynomial: the particular solution has the same type (undetermined coefficients); the complementary $ce^x$ blows up, so a bounded-type condition or a point condition fixes $c$.
$\int e^{ax}\sin bx\,dx=\frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx-b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2}$; here $a=-1,\ b=1$.
Check: $y=-1-2(\sin x+\cos x)$ gives $y'-y=-2(\cos x-\sin x)+1+2(\sin x+\cos x)=1+4\sin x$ ✓.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(x+y+2)^2dx=dy$; $y(0)=-2$. Let the maximum and minimum values of the function $y=y(x)$ in $\left[0,\frac\pi3\right]$ be $\alpha$ and $\beta$, respectively. If $(3\alpha+\pi)^2+\beta^2=\gamma+\delta\sqrt3$, $\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb Z$, then $\gamma+\delta$ equals ________.
questions.key_idea: $t=x+y+2$ gives $\frac{dt}{dx}=1+t^2$, so $y=\tan x-x-2$, which is increasing since $y'=\tan^2x\ge0$.
useful_results: For $y'=f(ax+by+c)$ put $t=ax+by+c$; the equation becomes separable: $t'=a+bf(t)$.
$\int\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\tan^{-1}t$: here $t'=1+t^2$ gives $t=\tan(x+c)$, so $y=\tan(x+c)-x-2$.
Extrema of a monotone function on a closed interval are at the endpoints: $y'=\tan^2x\ge0$.

questions.question: Let $f$ be a differentiable function in the interval $(0,\infty)$ such that $f(1)=1$ and $\lim_{t\to x}\frac{t^2f(x)-x^2f(t)}{t-x}=1$ for each $x>0$. Then $2f(2)+3f(3)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The limit is a derivative: $\frac{t^2f(x)-x^2f(t)}{t-x}\to2xf(x)-x^2f'(x)$, giving a linear equation.
solution: The numerator vanishes at $t=x$, so apply L'Hospital's rule (differentiate with respect to $t$): the limit is $\lim_{t\to x}\frac{2tf(x)-x^2f'(t)}{1}=2xf(x)-x^2f'(x)$.
$\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{2y}{x}=-\frac1{x^2}$, a linear equation with integrating factor $e^{-\int\frac2xdx}=\frac1{x^2}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF writes the limit as 'lim_{x->infinity}' (it should be t -> x) in its first working line; the rest of the working (differentiate w.r.t. t, 2xy - x^2 y' = 1) is right and gives the same answer 24.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the numerator as $x^2t^2\left[g(x)-g(t)\right]$ with $g=\frac{f}{x^2}$: the limit is $-x^4g'(x)$ - an exact derivative, no L'Hospital.

useful_results: A limit $\lim_{t\to x}\frac{A(t,x)}{t-x}$ with $A(x,x)=0$ is $\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}\big|_{t=x}$; recognise a difference quotient before using L'Hospital.
$\lim_{t\to x}\frac{t^kf(x)-x^kf(t)}{t-x}=x^{k+2}\cdot\left(-\frac{d}{dx}\frac{f(x)}{x^k}\right)$: the quotient $\frac f{x^k}$ is the natural variable.
Check: $f(x)=\frac1{3x}+\frac23x^2$ gives $2xf-x^2f'=\frac23+\frac43x^3-x^2\left(-\frac1{3x^2}+\frac43x\right)=1$ ✓.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{2x}{(1+x^2)^2}y=xe^{\frac1{1+x^2}}$; $y(0)=0$. Then the area enclosed by the curve $f(x)=y(x)e^{-\frac1{1+x^2}}$ and the line $y-x=4$ is ________.
questions.key_idea: The integrating factor $e^{-1/(1+x^2)}$ makes $f(x)=ye^{-1/(1+x^2)}=\frac{x^2}2$ appear directly: a parabola and a line.
solution: The curve $y=\frac{x^2}{2}$ and the line $y=x+4$ meet where $\frac{x^2}2=x+4$, i.e. $x^2-2x-8=0$, $x=-2,\ 4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the parabola-chord area formula: the area between a parabola $y=ax^2+\ldots$ and a chord is $\frac{|a|\,(x_2-x_1)^3}{6}$.
solution: After $f(x)=\frac{x^2}2$ and the intersections $x=-2,\ 4$ are found, the region is the segment cut from the parabola $y=\frac{x^2}{2}$ by the chord $y=x+4$.
Area of a parabolic segment $=\frac{|a|(x_2-x_1)^3}{6}$ with $a=\frac12$ and $x_2-x_1=6$.

useful_results: Area between the parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c$ and a chord meeting it at $x_1,x_2$ is $\frac{|a|(x_2-x_1)^3}{6}$ (Archimedes).
When $P=\frac{g'}{g}\cdot$ (something) the integrating factor often cancels the right side: here $e^{-1/(1+x^2)}$ cancels $e^{1/(1+x^2)}$, so the right side becomes $x$.
The curve asked about is $f=ye^{-1/(1+x^2)}$, not $y$: re-read what is being plotted.

questions.question: Let a conic $C$ pass through the point $(4,-2)$ and $P(x,y)$, $x\ge3$, be any point on $C$. Let the slope of the line touching the conic $C$ only at a single point $P$ be half the slope of the line joining the points $P$ and $(3,-5)$. If the focal distance of the point $(7,1)$ on $C$ is $d$, then $12d$ equals ________.
questions.key_idea: The slope condition is $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y+5}{2(x-3)}$; separating gives the parabola $(y+5)^2=9(x-3)$.
solution: The slope of the tangent at $P$ is $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac12\cdot\frac{y+5}{x-3}$.
The point $(7,1)$ lies on $C$: $(1+5)^2=36=9(7-3)$ ✓. Focal distance $d=\sqrt{\left(7-\frac{21}4\right)^2+(1+5)^2}=\sqrt{\frac{49}{16}+36}=\sqrt{\frac{625}{16}}=\frac{25}4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Focal distance equals the distance from the directrix: $x_P+a'$ for a parabola with vertex at $x=3$ and $a'=\frac94$ - no distance formula.
solution: $(y+5)^2=9(x-3)$ is a parabola opening to the right with vertex $(3,-5)$ and $4a=9$, $a=\frac94$.
Focal distance of $(7,1)$ = its distance from the directrix $=7-\frac34=\frac{25}4$ (equivalently $(x-3)+a=4+\frac94$).

useful_results: For the parabola $(y-k)^2=4a(x-h)$ the focal distance of any point $P(x_0,y_0)$ is $x_0-h+a$ (distance from the directrix $x=h-a$).
$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y-k}{m(x-h)}$ has solutions $|y-k|^{m}=C|x-h|$; $m=2$ gives a parabola with horizontal axis through $(h,k)$ as vertex.
The condition $x\ge3$ is the branch of $(y+5)^2=9(x-3)$ that is a function of $x$ on each half; the whole curve is the parabola.

questions.question: If the solution $y(x)$ of the given differential equation $(e^y+1)\cos x\,dx+e^y\sin x\,dy=0$ passes through the point $\left(\frac\pi2,0\right)$, then the value of $e^{y\left(\frac\pi6\right)}$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Divide by $(e^y+1)\sin x$: $\cot x\,dx+\frac{e^y}{e^y+1}dy=0$ integrates to $\sin x\,(e^y+1)=c$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The equation is exact: $M=(e^y+1)\cos x$, $N=e^y\sin x$ have $M_y=N_x=e^y\cos x$, and $\sin x\,(e^y+1)$ is the potential.
solution: With $M=(e^y+1)\cos x$ and $N=e^y\sin x$: $\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=e^y\cos x=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}$, so the equation is exact.

useful_results: $d\left[(e^y+1)\sin x\right]=(e^y+1)\cos x\,dx+e^y\sin x\,dy$: the left side of the equation is an exact differential.
Exactness test: $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ is exact iff $M_y=N_x$; then $\varphi=\int M\,dx+h(y)$.
A question asking for $e^{y}$ (not $y$) is a hint that the solution is naturally $e^y=\ldots$.

questions.question: Let $\alpha|x|=|y|e^{xy-\beta}$, $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N$ be the solution of the differential equation $x\,dy-y\,dx+xy(x\,dy+y\,dx)=0$, $y(1)=2$. Then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: Divide by $xy$: $\frac{dy}{y}-\frac{dx}{x}+d(xy)=0$.
useful_results: $x\,dy+y\,dx=d(xy)$ and $\frac{dy}{y}-\frac{dx}{x}=d\ln\left|\frac yx\right|$: dividing by $xy$ separates the equation into exact differentials.
The first integral is $\ln\left|\frac yx\right|+xy=c$, i.e. $|y|e^{xy}=C|x|$.
Natural numbers $\alpha,\beta$ are fixed by matching $2|x|=|y|e^{xy-2}$ with the given form.

questions.question: For a differentiable function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, suppose $f'(x)=3f(x)+\alpha$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $f(0)=1$ and $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=7$. Then $9f(-\log_e3)$ is equal to ________.
questions.key_idea: The solution $f=\frac{(3+\alpha)e^{3x}-\alpha}{3}$ tends to $-\frac\alpha3$ as $x\to-\infty$, which must equal $7$.

alternate_solutions.idea: If $f\to7$ at $-\infty$ then $f'\to0$, so $3\cdot7+\alpha=0$; and $f-7$ then satisfies $g'=3g$.
solution: As $x\to-\infty$, $f\to7$ and (since $f$ and $f'=3f+\alpha$ both have limits and $f$ is bounded) $f'\to0$: $3(7)+\alpha=0$, so $\alpha=-21$.

useful_results: For $f'=kf+\alpha$ ($k>0$) every solution tends to the equilibrium $-\frac\alpha k$ as $x\to-\infty$ (the other term $e^{kx}\to0$); the limit at $-\infty$ therefore identifies $\alpha$.
A function with a finite limit and whose derivative has a limit has derivative limit $0$.
Contrast with the Jan-2024 paper (Q36 here): there the condition $f\to1$ at $-\infty$ was inconsistent with the sign of the exponent; here $k=3>0$ and the data are consistent.
